edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. V, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 28)

source_text: Si quis dicit: alius est filius Dei ante saecula, et alius qui extremis temporibus apparuit; et non confitetur unum et eundem esse illum ante saecula, et qui novissimis temporibus apparuit, sicut scriptum est; anathema sit. Quomodo dici potest alius filius Dei ante saecula, et alius in extremis temporibus; cum ipse Dominus dicat: Antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum. Et, quia a patre exivi, et venio; et iterum vado ad patrem meum?
thought_title: The Son before the ages and the Son of the last times are one
orientation: Gregory condemns splitting the Son before the ages from the one who appeared in the last times, and answers from Christ's own sayings in John.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone says: one (alius) is the son of God before the ages (ante saecula), and another (alius) who appeared (apparuit) in the last times (extremis temporibus); and does not confess that one and the same (unum et eundem) is he before the ages and he who appeared in the latest times (novissimis temporibus), as it is written; let him be anathema. How can it be said [that] the son of God before the ages [is] one, and another in the last times, when the Lord himself says: Before Abraham came to be (fieret), I am (ego sum). And, that I went out (exivi) from the father, and I come (venio); and again I go (vado) to my father?

choices.why: Masculine: two subjects, without importing the later term 'person'.
Present tense of this text kept against the Vulgate's veni.

bible_refs.note: quoted: Antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum
quoted loosely: a patre exivi, et venio; et iterum vado ad patrem meum

pass_b_english: If anyone says, “The Son of God before the ages is someone other than the one who appeared in the last times,” and does not confess that the one before the ages and the one who appeared in the last times are one and the same, as it is written, let him be anathema.

How can it be said that the Son of God before the ages is someone other than the one in the last times, when the Lord himself says, “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58), and, “I came forth from the Father, and I am coming; and again I am going to my Father” (John 16:28)?
notes: Alius … alius (masculine) rendered “someone other than”, which keeps the point that the heresy makes two subjects, without adding the later word “person”.
The second saying is a loose form of John 16:28 (Vulgate exivi a Patre et veni in mundum … vado ad Patrem); the present venio (“I am coming”) of this text is kept.
“As it is written” in the anathema has no single target and is left uncited.
